## Conversation Context

**Zero athletes in the entire 99 have a second test.** So test-retest reliability cannot be estimated from this dataset at all.

That matters because of v1's own finding: a ~3 SD range across 9 categories appears *by chance*. An athlete's highest and lowest categories may be noise. Without a standard error of measurement, you cannot tell a stable trait peak from a bad day — and handing a coach an individual profile built on that would repeat precisely the error v1 caught.

**The fix is cheap and specific: ask S2 for test-retest reliability or SEM per subtest.** With it you compute a reliable-change threshold — the minimum gap between two of an athlete's categories that exceeds measurement error. That converts "his top category is improvisation" into "his improvisation is *reliably* above his decision complexity," which is a defensible coaching statement. Failing that, retest 10–15 athletes and estimate it yourself.

This is worth doing, because it's the analysis that actually delivers your original goal — individualized coaching cues, the option you called the near neighbor in round 1. It just can't be done honestly yet.

## The scope in short

**`docs/V2-SCOPE.md`** — three tracks, and the headline is that only one is unblocked.

**Track A — pooled, position-adjusted (unblocked).** Model expected profile from position across ~92 athletes instead of comparing each player to a room mean built on 8–15. Two real gains: far more stable estimates, and the nine small rooms stop being excluded. Adds the speed/accuracy measures V1 never touched.

I'd rather be honest about its value than oversell it: V1 found the OL room *less* extreme than chance, so this will likely return nulls too. That's still worth buying — "all 92 checked with a calibrated method, no outliers" closes the question instead of leaving it to be re-asked every cycle.

**Track B — individual reliable-change profiles (blocked).** This is the one that delivers what you originally asked for. Not "is he unusual" but "is his improvisation *reliably* above his decision complexity" — a within-athlete claim needing no comparison to anyone. Blocked on SEM, because V1 proved a ~3 SD range appears by chance.

**Track C — is the position gradient real (blocked).** Needs S2's positional norms.

## The recommendation

**The next action is an email to S2, not an analysis.** Four asks, and one of them matters no matter which track you run: whether the normative database was revised between 2022 and 2026. Five of your linemen tested before this year, and a quietly revised norm would put their percentiles on a different scale entirely — a confound V1 had no way to check.

Send it today, start Track A while waiting. If S2 won't supply reliability, retesting 12–15 athletes is the cheaper route to Track B.

The three "parse failures" weren't failures — all three are punters/kickers yielding exactly 7 values with zero `N/A`. **P/K runs a reduced battery.** They can't join a nine-category pooled model.

And the **speed/accuracy secondary measures extract from 96 of 99 reports**. V1 pulled 10 of 12 available values per athlete and discarded the pair that's arguably most coachable — "fast but inaccurate under pressure" is something a position coach can actually act on.

Given the pre-registration argument — a timestamped commit is only as durable as the disk it's on — say the word and I'll create a private GitHub repo and push it. **The email to S2** is the highest-leverage next action and nothing I can do for you. Four asks in `V2-SCOPE.md`; the one that matters regardless of which track you run is whether the normative database was revised between 2022 and 2026, since five of your linemen tested before this year.

## The five asks, in priority order

**1. Test-retest reliability or SEM, per category.** This is the big one. It's what unblocks the individual profiles you actually wanted. Ask for the ICC or test-retest correlation *and* the standard error of measurement for each of the 9 categories plus the speed/accuracy measures — ideally over a realistic interval (weeks to months) in a comparable population. Without it you cannot say a player's improvisation is genuinely above his decision complexity rather than a good day on one task.

**2. Was the normative database revised between 2022 and 2026?** This one threatens work already done. Five of your linemen tested before this year. If S2 re-based their norms in between, those percentiles aren't on the same scale as the 2026 cohort, and the room mean V1 computed is partly an artifact. Cheap question, potentially expensive answer.

**3. Positional norms within the reference population.** Do offensive linemen score lower than defensive backs generally? Without this you cannot tell whether your 42nd-percentile OL room is a Baylor fact or a property of the instrument.

**4. What exactly is "NFL PROSPECTS — ALL POSITIONS"?** How many athletes, from which years, selected how. See below — this changes the reading of every number you have.

**5. Why does the P/K battery have 7 measures instead of 9?** Which are omitted, and why. Determines whether kickers can be partially pooled or must stay separate.

## One thing worth knowing before you send

Your reference group is **NFL prospects** — a heavily selected elite population, not college players. That reframes things. Your team mean sits at the **59th percentile of NFL prospects**, and only two rooms fall below the 50th. Read plainly, your athletes are testing above the median NFL prospect on these measures.

V1 never surfaced this because it was scoped to one room and hunting for outliers. It's arguably the most presentable thing in the dataset — and it's exactly why ask #4 matters, because the claim is only as good as the composition of that norm.

## While you wait

**Run the research track first — it may answer ask #1 without S2.** The original routing brief recommended `/research` on S2's construct validity in parallel with the grilling, and it never ran. S2 has published on draft prediction, so reliability coefficients may already exist in the literature. If they do, Track B unblocks immediately and you stop waiting on an email.

**Then Track A prep**, which needs nothing from S2: harden the extractor for the P/K layout and the invalid report, add the speed/accuracy dimensions, and — per the standing rule from ADR 0013 — pre-register and commit Track A's thresholds *before* running it. Same discipline, same reason.

**Contingency worth deciding now:** if S2 won't share reliability, retesting 12–15 athletes gives you an in-house estimate. Fall camp may be the practical window, which makes it a scheduling question rather than an analysis one.

Want me to draft the email to S2, or kick off the research track? I'd do both — the email is short, and the research can run while you send it.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User approved pushing the vault harvest, committing the three untracked vault files, and creating a private GitHub repo for `S2_Evaluation`.

**Decisions Made:**
- Harvest shipped: one ledger row + three Knowledge articles (calibrate-the-threshold-against-a-null, timestamp-the-threshold-under-self-review, vendor-percentiles-only-comparable-within-reference-group), committed `2dd4189`, vault pushed at `e399ba2`.
- V2 scoped in `docs/V2-SCOPE.md` (commit `77355dc`) as three tracks: **Track A** pooled position-adjusted model across ~92 athletes (unblocked, likely null but closes the question); **Track B** individual reliable-change profiles (blocked on SEM/test-retest reliability); **Track C** positional gradient (blocked on S2's positional norms).

**Lessons Learned:**
- Zero athletes have a second test, so test-retest reliability/SEM cannot be estimated from this dataset — without it, an individual's high vs. low category gap may be pure noise (V1 showed ~3 SD range appears by chance).
- The three "parse failures" (Sullivan_Riley, Williams_Palmer, mueller_bronson) were not bugs — all three are punters/kickers running a **reduced 7-measure battery with zero N/A**, so P/K cannot join a 9-category pooled model.
- Speed/accuracy secondary measures extract from **96 of 99** reports; V1 pulled 10 of 12 available values and discarded arguably the most coachable pair ("fast but inaccurate under pressure").
- Reference group is **NFL prospects**, a heavily selected elite population — team mean sits at the 59th percentile, only two rooms below 50th. V1 never surfaced this because it was scoped to one room hunting outliers.
- PII audit gotcha: full-history blob scan hit `roberts`, which was a substring of the *Robertson et al. 2017* citation — word-boundary re-scan found zero real names.
- zsh glob-expanded the `?` in a GitHub API URL, producing a **false pass** on the "no data paths on remote" check. Quote URLs containing `?` before grepping the result.

**Action Items:**
